Chapter 8: Empowering Others—Principle-Centered Leadership at Home and Work
So, once you’ve started to get clear on your own priorities, the next step just feels natural—helping the people around you do the same. Whether you’re a parent, a partner, a manager, or just a good friend, you’ve got this unique chance to create spaces where folks can really focus on what matters most to them.
Let’s talk about leadership as stewardship. This isn’t about controlling every move—far from it. Principle-centered leadership means you’re a steward, guiding others as they discover and act on their own values and strengths. That’s how you build trust, real collaboration, and a sense of shared purpose.
Imagine a great coach. Instead of barking out orders, they help each player figure out their own strengths and how they fit into the team. By giving people room to grow and make decisions, the whole team becomes stronger and more resilient.
So, how do you actually empower others? Here are a few ideas:
First, try modeling Quadrant II living yourself. Show the people around you what it looks like to focus on what’s important, even if it’s not urgent. Next, encourage some real reflection. Ask open-ended questions—ones that help others get clear on their own values and goals.
When it comes to delegating, give people responsibility, and trust them to figure out the best way to get things done. And don’t forget to celebrate progress—every small win deserves acknowledgment. That positive energy? It’s contagious.
Now, let’s zoom out and look at the bigger picture—building principle-centered cultures in your family or at work. When everyone’s on the same page about what really matters, it creates unity and direction.
One way to do this is by creating a family or team mission statement. Work together to define what you care about most and how you want to support each other. Then, make space for regular check-ins—honest conversations where you talk about priorities, challenges, and even celebrate those small successes.
It also helps to put supportive systems in place. Maybe it’s routines, rituals, or even some helpful policies that make it easier for everyone to focus on their top priorities.
For example, imagine a family that sets aside Sunday evenings to plan the week together. Everyone’s voice gets heard, and the week feels a little less chaotic. Or, picture a workplace where employees are encouraged to block off time for learning or creative projects—that sends a strong message about what’s really valued.
When you empower others, you’re not just making a difference in your own life—you’re starting a ripple effect of positive change. Principle-centered living becomes something bigger than yourself, and those ripples can reach farther than you might ever imagine.
